speaker: Emily Heyward
title: EMILY HEYWARD: Build A Brand People Love (The Red Antler Way)
question: In early-stage consumer brand research, why do surveys and focus groups often fail to uncover a target audience's true mindset?
guest: I'm glad you're asking 'cause I think there's a lot of very bad consumer research out there, and I've definitely met a lot of founders, particularly those who come from a more data-minded place, who just want to run a survey and prove that there's a need for their business. That's fine if you're in the early stages and just trying to test market size—sure, run a survey to see if these people actually exist. But once you're in the phase of really identifying your target audience and their deeper mindset, qualitative research—speaking to a smaller set of people in direct, deeper conversations—can actually be much more valuable than quantitative research going for a statistically significant sample. We typically do it in the form of one-on-one phone calls, which is the most efficient way to reach a geographically diverse set of people. My problem with focus groups is you get a group of people in the room and they can often be subject to groupthink, or you have one dominant person influencing everyone else. One-on-one conversations are the best way to go beneath the surface and really listen and probe to understand what's behind what they're saying.

points.core: Surveys capture surface validation rather than the deeper emotional drivers behind behavior.
points.note: Accept: quantitative surveys test market size or demand existence but miss underlying psychology, motivations, or beliefs. Do not credit: claiming surveys are always useless or biased.

points.core: Focus groups distort honest feedback because social dynamics trigger conformity among participants.
points.note: Accept: groupthink, peer pressure, social desirability bias, or one dominant voice swaying the room. Do not credit: generic complaints about focus group cost or scheduling.

points.core: One-on-one interviews let researchers probe beneath surface statements to uncover hidden motives.
points.note: Accept: individual conversations allowing follow-up questions, digging past literal answers, or reading between the lines. Do not credit: simply stating that qualitative research is more personal.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Surveys and focus groups mostly capture what people say, not what they actually think, feel, or do, and in early-stage research that gap is the whole problem.

People are poor reporters of their own motivations. Much of buying behaviour is driven by habit, emotion, and identity, which respondents cannot easily access, so they offer plausible-sounding rationalisations instead. They also answer in ways that make them look sensible or virtuous (social desirability bias), and they overstate future intent: "I would buy that" rarely predicts a purchase.

The formats add their own distortions. Surveys confine answers to the researcher's categories and wording, so you only learn about what you already thought to ask, when early on you do not yet know the right questions. Focus groups are artificial settings where dominant voices, groupthink, and the desire to please the moderator shape what gets said. Both strip away the real context in which decisions happen.

That is why early-stage work tends to favour observation, one-on-one in-depth interviews, and analysis of unprompted behaviour and language, such as reviews, forums, and search data, with surveys used later to quantify hypotheses.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Surveys and focus groups often fail in early-stage consumer research because they capture stated intentions rather than actual behavior. Most purchasing decisions are driven by subconscious habits, emotions, and situational triggers that consumers cannot accurately introspect; when asked directly why they buy, people invent logical-sounding post-hoc rationalizations. Furthermore, social desirability bias leads participants to answer as their idealized, aspirational selves—claiming they prioritize sustainability, health, or craftsmanship—rather than admitting to convenience, status-seeking, or impulse. Focus groups compound this distortion through groupthink and moderator pleasing, where dominant personalities and the desire for social approval steer the room toward artificial consensus while silencing honest outliers. Meanwhile, early-stage surveys prematurely narrow discovery by forcing respondents into pre-defined options that merely reflect the brand’s existing assumptions and blind spots, missing unarticulated pain points entirely. Finally, both methods take place in a sterile, hypothetical vacuum detached from real-world context. Saying a concept sounds appealing in a compensated session carries zero cost compared to trading scarce attention, money, and ingrained routines at the actual moment of purchase.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Surveys and focus groups mostly capture what people *say*, and that is often different from what they actually think, feel, and do. A lot of what drives consumer behavior is emotional, habitual or unconscious, so people can't reliably explain it when asked. When they try, they tend to give tidy, rational-sounding reasons after the fact.

Both formats also add their own distortions. People give socially acceptable answers and try to please the moderator. In focus groups, one or two confident voices can steer everyone else toward agreement. Surveys are limited by the researcher's own assumptions: fixed questions and answer options only measure what the brand already thought to ask, so unexpected motivations stay hidden. And because the setting is artificial and cut off from real buying moments, you get hypothetical intentions ("I'd definitely buy that") that rarely predict real behavior.

That's why early-stage brand work often relies on ethnography, in-home or in-context observation, social listening, diary studies and one-on-one in-depth interviews. These methods show how people actually live, the words they use and the tensions they deal with, which together give a truer picture of their mindset.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Surveys and focus groups often miss a target audience’s true mindset because they rely on what people say rather than what they actually do. Consumers frequently struggle to articulate subconscious habits, emotional triggers, and unspoken trade-offs, leading them to offer neat, post-hoc rationalizations instead of their real motivations. In focus groups, social desirability bias and groupthink compound this problem: participants conform to dominant voices, censor awkward truths, and try to appear thoughtful or agreeable to the moderator. Surveys introduce a different distortion by forcing respondents into the researcher’s predefined framing, which can confirm existing assumptions while overlooking how people naturally think and talk about their problems. Both methods also strip away real-world context. Asking hypothetical questions in a questionnaire or conference room removes the situational friction, budget constraints, and social cues that shape genuine purchasing behavior. As a result, early-stage brands often walk away with polite, surface-level feedback that fails to predict how consumers will actually feel or act in the wild.

models.answer:
Surveys and focus groups often capture what people say they want under research conditions. People may sincerely misremember what drove a purchase, struggle to put a habit or emotion into words, or give an answer that sounds more sensible or socially acceptable. In focus groups, a confident participant can steer the conversation and make others less willing to disagree.

Early in brand research, you may still be learning which needs matter and how customers describe them. A survey’s preset questions and answer choices can impose your assumptions before you’ve heard theirs. And asking what someone *would* buy strips away the real-life context—price, time pressure, habit, and competing options—that shapes what they actually choose. Observing people in that context and asking about specific recent decisions can reveal motivations that abstract questions miss.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Surveys and focus groups ask people to explain choices they often make out of habit, on a feeling, or in response to a particular situation. Someone may sincerely say they buy a brand for its quality yet overlook how often they reach for it because the packaging feels familiar. When asked why, they give the reason that comes most readily to mind.

In early-stage research, the team is still learning what matters to its audience. A survey can bake the team’s assumptions into its answer choices, leaving people little room to describe a concern the researchers never considered. In a focus group, the first confident answer can steer the conversation, and people may soften opinions they’d express privately. Both methods can reveal how consumers talk about a brand, but understanding what drives their choices often requires seeing those choices in context.
